title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again
gist: Ars Technica's automotive editor is skeptical of Tesla's new Roadster reveal (383 mph, 0-60 in 0.8 seconds, production by 2028), citing Musk's history of overpromising, existing EVs like the McMurtry Spéirling that outperform the claims, and a weakening Tesla core business. The article also flags a possible Tesla-SpaceX merger that would give SpaceX access to the S&P 500.

insights.claim: Tesla's new Roadster uses stunt-style compressed nitrogen jets (100,000 psi) from four rear exhaust-like pipes, rear-wheel drive, 4680 cells with a special chemistry, and claimed 383 mph top speed and 0-60 mph in 0.8 seconds.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Specs are claims only, and the nitrogen-jet legality on roads is unresolved per the author.

insights.claim: Musk says the Roadster will enter production by 2028, but he has a long history of overpromising and underdelivering, including a 2017 claim that Tesla was making it already, free referral cars that never arrived and $50,000 deposits that proved hard to recover.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Discount the 2028 date and Tesla product-timeline claims; deposit liabilities are a reputational risk.
insights.quote: long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering

insights.claim: The Tesla 2 G lateral claim and performance targets are bested by existing EVs: the McMurtry Spéirling generates up to 3.5 lateral Gs, can drive upside down, beat an F1 car's lap time on the Top Gear track and set Goodwood hill record, with at least 24 of 100 planned cars sold.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Tesla's performance halo is no longer unique, weakening the point of the car.
insights.locator: You want to drive upside down?

insights.claim: There is not much market for very expensive, very fast EVs, because hypercar buyers want noise and an emotional connection that EVs don't deliver.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Low demand reduces the Roadster's commercial relevance beyond marketing.
insights.locator: And it’s not like there’s actually much of a market

insights.claim: Tesla's profits are vanishing even in quarters with decent sales as costs rise and selling prices drop, and most recent sales have not been decent.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Margin compression plus falling volume undermines earnings support for the valuation.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble

insights.claim: Tesla's valuation was built largely on promises of constant growth, but Europe and China now offer hundreds of EV models of which Tesla offers two, the Models 3 and Y are aging, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate as rapidly as the Chinese brands taking its share; it might even leave the Chinese market.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Competitive erosion in China and Europe challenges the growth premise in the valuation.
insights.quote: Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth

insights.claim: Musk appears more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX, claiming AI synergies although most of his AI-derived revenues come from renting GPU time to others.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Merger rationale rests on a thin AI revenue story, so watch for governance and dilution issues.
insights.locator: But as Musk has told us time and again

insights.claim: A Tesla-SpaceX merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500, which rejected the rocket company in June because inclusion requires several consecutive profitable quarters, unlocking billions from passive funds; the article says this could happen before year end.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Index inclusion would drive passive buying; monitor merger news for index-flow effects on both stocks.
insights.locator: But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor
